drills.q: How many threads are in a warp on an NVIDIA GPU?
options: Whatever `blockDim.x` is set to
drills.why: Thirty-two is a fixed property of the hardware, not something you configure. It comes from graphics: the SM controller grouped eight 2x2 pixel quads into one warp, and eight quads of four pixels is 32.

drills.q: Why is a warp 32 threads wide rather than some other number?
options: It is the widest a scheduler can decode in one cycle
It is eight 2x2 pixel quads, and quads exist because mipmap selection
It matches the 32-bit register width
It was chosen to match the cache line size
drills.why: The number is inherited from texture filtering. A derivative is cheapest as a difference against a neighbour, so fragments are shaded in quads, and the Tesla paper describes the SM controller grouping eight quads into a warp.

drills.q: A block of 33 threads occupies how many warps?
options: One, since 33 is close enough to 32
Two, and 31 lanes of the second warp are idle
Two, and both are fully occupied
It fails to launch
drills.why: Warps are allocated whole. The remaining 31 lanes are masked off and still take their slot in the scheduler, which is why block sizes are almost always multiples of 32.

drills.q: Why prefer `warpSize` over writing the literal 32?
options: The compiler cannot fold the literal
`warpSize` is a runtime value, and the same concept is 64 wide on other
The literal is undefined inside device code
It has no effect either way, so it is only a style preference
drills.why: Writing 32 works today on NVIDIA hardware and gives the wrong answer the moment the same idea is read against a vendor whose warp is wider. Reading warpSize says what you meant rather than what happened to be true.

drills.q: Half the threads in a warp take one side of a branch and half take the other. How long does the warp take?
options: The longer of the two sides
The sum of both sides
Half of each side, since half the lanes are idle
The shorter side, because the rest are masked off
drills.why: A warp has one instruction pointer for 32 lanes. It runs one side with the disagreeing lanes masked, then the other with the mask inverted. Nothing overlaps, so the costs add.

drills.q: A branch that exactly 50% of your threads take is:
options: Always expensive, because half the lanes are idle
Free if the split lands on warp boundaries, and expensive if it
Always free, because the scheduler regroups the lanes
Expensive only on pre-Volta hardware
drills.why: Divergence is spatial rather than statistical. A CPU asks whether a branch is predictable in time; a GPU asks whether it is uniform in space.

drills.q: What changed about warps from Volta onward?
options: Warps became 64 threads wide
Each thread got its own program counter and call stack, so lockstep
Divergence became free
Warps were replaced by blocks as the unit of execution
drills.why: This is why the warp intrinsics carry a _sync suffix and an explicit mask. You now have to name the lanes you mean, because the hardware no longer guarantees they arrive together.

drills.q: Two blocks in the same kernel need to exchange a value. What should you do?
options: Use `__syncthreads()` between them
Put the value in shared memory
Split the work into two kernel launches
Spin on a flag in global memory until the other block writes it
drills.why: There is no ordering between blocks and no barrier across them. A block that waits on another can deadlock, because the block it waits for may not be scheduled until the waiting block finishes.

drills.q: Why is the absence of communication between blocks useful rather than merely restrictive?
options: It makes kernels shorter to write
It lets the same kernel run unchanged on a GPU with 20 SMs or 148, and
It removes the need for shared memory
It guarantees deterministic output ordering
drills.why: Every scheduling decision belongs to the hardware, and it can only belong to the hardware because you promised not to care about the order.

drills.q: Putting `__syncthreads()` inside a branch that only some threads take is:
options: Fine, as long as the branch is uniform within each warp
Undefined behaviour, and in practice hangs
A compile error
Slower, but correct
drills.why: Every thread in the block has to reach the barrier. The threads that skipped it never arrive, and the ones that did wait forever.

drills.q: Why is switching between warps on an SM nearly free, when switching threads on a CPU is expensive?
options: The GPU has no operating system to involve
Every resident warp keeps its own registers for as long as it lives, so
Warps are lighter because they share a program counter
The scheduler switches only when a warp finishes
drills.why: The register file is a context store, not a cache. A CPU saves and restores registers because they belong to the core; an SM has enough of them to give every resident warp its own.

drills.q: More resident warps on an SM means:
options: More switching overhead, as on a CPU
More chances to hide a stall, since the SM issues from a different warp
Slower execution once the count exceeds the number of cores
No difference, since only one warp issues per cycle
drills.why: This inverts the CPU intuition. Threads are not a cost to be managed; they are the mechanism by which a several-hundred-cycle memory wait disappears behind work that was going to happen anyway.

drills.q: What limits how many warps can be resident on an SM?
options: The number of CUDA cores
Finite resources such as the register file, so the registers each thread
The size of the L2 cache
The grid size you launched with
drills.why: This is the price of the register-file-as-context-store design. Using too many registers per thread quietly reduces the number of warps available to hide latency.

options: Shared memory and a barrier
Global memory
Registers directly, with no memory and no barrier
The L1 cache
drills.why: Because a warp executes together, lanes can hand each other register contents. Five shuffle steps reduce 32 values to one in lane 0, which is log2(32).

drills.q: Why is a grid-stride loop usually better than one thread per element?
options: It runs faster on every input size
It decouples the grid from the problem, so one launch configuration
It removes the need for a bounds check
It avoids divergence entirely
drills.why: The property worth having is that the same kernel is debuggable serially and fast in parallel. One block of one thread still gives the right answer.
